extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate mathematics instructors (RUME/MAA community)
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric-style criteria and findings for classroom practices and research methods in undergraduate, proof-based mathematics courses (including use of Toulmin analysis, linguistic registers for definitions, and conjecturing/skepticism). Useful for researchers studying instruction or instructors seeking evidence-based practices to support student understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation between linguistic registers
rubrics_metrics.description: "Translation across these registers provided a mechanism by which some students were able to segue their concept image and concept definitions successfully."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit translation among metaphorical, common, and symbolic registers in classroom dialogue and activities so students can connect their concept image to formal concept definitions; examples in the paper include the party metaphor for sequence convergence and translating 'close enough / far enough' into epsilon/index notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three registers of definition articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The classroom discussion used three linguistic registers: (1) metaphorical register, (2) common register, and (3) symbolic register (examples: arrows metaphor / 'no two inputs have the same output' / formal symbolic if f(x1)=f(x2) then x1=x2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and name these registers when presenting definitions; each register embodies different aspects (idea/concept image vs. formal definition) and should be leveraged intentionally during instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the duality of 'idea' (concept image) and 'definition' (formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The dialogue separately referenced the 'idea' and the 'definition.' The 'idea' was usually expressed using the metaphorical or common register, while the 'definition' arrived by the end of the discussion in the symbolic register."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly separate and label the informal 'idea' and the formal 'definition' during instruction; use the informal registers to build concept image before presenting the symbolic definition to promote harmonisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors/common register to build concept image, then shift to symbolic primacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors and common language help students develop their concept image; over time students should be guided to give more prominence to the formal, symbolic definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce metaphors (e.g., 'party' for sequence limits) and common-language explanations, then demonstrate and translate to symbolic form; monitor over-time shift in student preference/primacy toward symbolic representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing non-standard heuristics without translating to formal definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The professor's non-standard criterion of a 'steepest point' for uniform continuity produced student misconceptions until students translated the formal definition into the common register and corrected their image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using informal heuristics or novel metaphors, explicitly translate them to/from the formal definition; check for misconceptions that can arise when students construct concept images and definitions simultaneously for unfamiliar topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided reinvention with conjecturing to transition informal→formal
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used 'guided reinvention incorporating frequent student conjectures' where students developed and wrote conjectures and were encouraged to resolve or refine them, using skepticism to suspend judgment and explore alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences of tasks and interviews that prompt students to make conjectures, test, refine, and resolve them; use guided reinvention as a pedagogical pathway from intuitive to formal understanding (example: reinventing Dirichlet function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tasks that generate useful uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Zaslavsky's three types of mathematical tasks that lead to uncertainty: competing claims; unknown paths or questionable conclusions; and non-readily verifiable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or craft tasks that evoke one or more of these uncertainty types to stimulate reflective thinking and productive skepticism in students; use contextual problems to complement conjecturing activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster skepticism as 'suspending judgment' during inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Brown: skepticism described as 'suspending judgment against a backdrop of empirical or experiential evidence'—a classroom practice allowing students to explore and refine conjectures while withholding premature acceptance/rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to adopt skepticism (doubt coupled with a belief about truth value) as a stance during problem solving and conjecturing, enabling deeper exploration and revision of initial metaphors and beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of skepticism/conjecturing to challenge naive metaphors (example: continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students holding a 'natural continuity' metaphor (continuity as motion) were able, via skepticism and conjecturing, to reinvent the Dirichlet function and alter their metaphor toward the formal (pointwise) notion of continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When students' embodied metaphors lead to incorrect generalizations (e.g., continuity only on open intervals), use guided tasks and skeptical inquiry to surface and revise these metaphors toward formal conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toulmin model for analyzing teaching (argumentation components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Toulmin’s (1969) model of argumentation to analyze instruction by categorizing arguments into data, warrant, backing, qualifier, or conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Toulmin analysis to both written and spoken classroom arguments to characterize instructor modeling; this analysis can be used as a predictor of subsequent student proof-writing performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for logging proof-production incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: "An incident was logged as such when any member of the class community was writing or showing a formal mathematical proof that drew on symbolic notation and logical reasoning."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting classroom research on proof instruction, log every episode meeting this criterion (written or presented proof with symbolic notation/logic) for subsequent analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include spoken as well as written argumentation when analyzing instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: Dr. Tripp always wrote data and conclusion, rarely wrote backing or qualifiers, and infrequently wrote warrants; however, when spoken comments were included, warrants appeared in more than half of all arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on written artifacts when analyzing instructor modeling—spoken warrants/backings may be present and are important for predicting student written behavior; document both modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor modeling completeness affects student uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper proposes that students will adopt argumentation methods modeled by the instructor; incomplete modeling (e.g., missing backing/qualifier in written models) may lead students to omit those aspects in their written proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To promote students' production of full argumentative structure in proofs, instructors should explicitly model all Toulmin components (data, warrant, backing, qualifier, conclusion) in the modalities students will be assessed on (especially written).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patterns from Toulmin-analysis of teaching to predict student proof-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of analysis developed via research ... has application ... This paper describes how that analysis can be used as a predictor of subsequent student proof-writing performance and shows that the predictions are reasonable approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the frequency/pattern of Toulmin components in instructor-presented proofs to patterns in student proofs to predict which argumentative elements students will appropriate; use this to inform targeted instructional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological criteria for classroom research on proofs/definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Study methods included observing all class meetings, keeping written records of dialogue and activities, weekly interviews with student volunteers, collection of demographic information, video review and logging of episodes, and analysis of student work on content assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching classroom practices in proof-based courses, adopt comprehensive data collection (full-course observation, recordings, regular interviews, artifacts, and assessments) to robustly link instruction to student performance.
